title: One blood
hook: Paul in Athens: all nations made of one blood, so contempt for a race denies the image of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gold ring, a filthy coat, and one good seat. Your line was the poor first. Whose name did you learn, and what did their week look like? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-three.

Paul is in Athens, and the city's thinkers have brought him up to the Areopagus to explain himself. He's been walking their streets, and he's found an altar with an inscription: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD." So he starts there, with something of theirs. Then, partway through, he says a sentence that reaches far past that hill. God, he says, "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." Not Athenians and then everyone else. Not one people as the original and the others as copies. One blood. Today, that sentence, and what it does to racism.

Paul's sentence stands on the first page of the Bible: "So God created man in his own image." Christians read that as true of every human face. Not some faces. Every one. Then Acts adds the family tree: one blood, all nations. Christians put the two together. If every person carries the image of God, and every nation shares one blood, then, in their reading, contempt for a race is contempt aimed at the image of God itself. That's why Christians who oppose racism call it a sin and not only bad manners. It denies something God made. Honesty matters here. Churches have not always lived this verse. Some Christians in history used the Bible to defend slavery and segregation. Other Christians, reading the same Bible, worked and suffered to end both, and they quoted lines like this one as they did. The verse didn't change. What changed was who was willing to hear it. Paul pushes it further in Galatians: "ye are all one in Christ Jesus." And in the last book of the Bible, John sees a vision of a great multitude "of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues" standing before the throne. Notice what's still there at the end. Nations. Tongues. The differences aren't erased. Christians read this as oneness that isn't sameness: one family, every accent kept.

Here's the practice: look at one face again. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose race or family story is different from yours: a coworker, a neighbor, a classmate, a voice you listen to. Ask yourself honestly what you've learned from them, and what you've never thought to ask. If a quick judgment about a whole group rises up while you sit, don't argue with it. Just name it, and set it down beside that one face. If you pray, you can give thanks for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
One blood. Paul's words in Athens: every nation shares one family, and every face carries the image of God.

Your line: one blood. Today, learn from someone whose story is different from yours, in a conversation, a book or a talk, and come away with one thing you didn't know before. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Christians teach this through the doctrine that every person bears the image of God; churches hold services and study groups on racial reconciliation, and some congregations deliberately bring together people of different races to worship side by side.

pairs: every nation and tongue still there

fork.setup: you're Paul, standing before the thinkers of Athens, who don't share your faith. where do you begin?
options: tell them their altars are worthless.
start with their own altar to the unknown god.
talk only about your own people's history.
fork.reveal: he starts with their altar, and a few lines later he even quotes their own poets: "For we are also his offspring." one blood, spoken to people he started by honoring.

original.note: Greek: blood; found in the Greek manuscripts behind the King James "of one blood" (Acts 17:26); many other manuscripts read simply "of one."

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about everyone getting along.
what it means: every nation shares one family and every face carries the image of God, so contempt for a race denies what God made.
what a scholar hears: Paul says it to a pagan audience, and in the next breath he quotes their own poets: "For we are also his offspring" (Acts 17:28).

notes: Historical statement: some Christians used the Bible to defend slavery and segregation, and other Christians worked to end both, quoting lines like Acts 17:26. Stated generally with no names, dates or counts; confirm the framing is fair and accurate.

Acts 17:26: the King James text reads 'of one blood'; some Greek manuscripts and many modern translations read 'from one' (man). The script and the original game quote the King James reading only. Confirm the original-language note is acceptable.
'Christians who oppose racism call it a sin': attributed to those who oppose it, not to all Christians. Confirm.
Revelation 7:9 is read as 'oneness that isn't sameness'; attributed to Christians as a reading. Confirm.
Editor: read in full; quotations checked against the KJV; no changes needed beyond this note.

Audit (2026-10-02): the image-of-God argument was voiced as the narrator's own logic ('hard to dodge'); now attributed to Christians' reading. Revelation 7:9 is a vision in the last book, not 'where it all ends'; teach and myth reworded. Original note on αἷμα now says the word is in the manuscripts behind the KJV and that many manuscripts read only 'of one'.
